result.summary: The armies meet and Alexandrus (Paris) is shamed by Hector into offering single combat with Menelaus for Helen. Oaths are sworn while Helen names the Achaean heroes for Priam. Menelaus nearly kills Alexandrus, but Venus rescues him and forces Helen to join him in bed, while Agamemnon claims victory.

scenes.title: Armies Meet; Hector Rebukes Paris
scenes.summary: The Trojans advance noisily and the Achaeans silently. Alexandrus shrinks from Menelaus and Hector scolds him.
scenes.stakes: Alexandrus risks disgrace and death; Menelaus hopes to avenge his wrong.

scenes.title: The Duel Proposed and Oaths Planned
scenes.summary: Alexandrus proposes single combat for Helen. Hector, Agamemnon and Menelaus agree and call for lambs and Priam.
scenes.stakes: The outcome of the whole war, and Helen's fate, rest on the duel and covenant.

scenes.title: Helen on the Wall
scenes.summary: Iris, disguised, summons Helen to the Scaean gates. She identifies Agamemnon, Ulysses, Ajax and Idomeneus for Priam, and Antenor recalls the embassy of Ulysses.
scenes.stakes: Helen faces shame and an uncertain fate as the prize of the duel.

scenes.title: The Oath Sworn
scenes.summary: Priam comes down, Agamemnon sacrifices the lambs and invokes the gods, and Priam returns to Ilius.
scenes.stakes: Oath-breakers risk divine punishment; Priam fears for his son.

scenes.title: Paris and Menelaus Fight
scenes.summary: Alexandrus throws first and fails. Menelaus's spear pierces the shield and his sword shatters. He drags Alexandrus by the helmet until Venus breaks the strap and carries Alexandrus off.
scenes.stakes: Alexandrus's life; Menelaus's chance at vengeance.

scenes.title: Venus, Helen and Paris
scenes.summary: Venus, disguised, lures Helen to Alexandrus's chamber. Helen reproaches him, then they lie together while Menelaus hunts him and Agamemnon claims victory.
scenes.stakes: Helen risks Venus's wrath and hatred; Troy risks breaking the oath.

alias_notes.explanation: Alexandrus and Paris are two names of the same Trojan prince.
A patronymic used for both Menelaus and Agamemnon.

notable_quotes.reason: Priam kindly blames the gods, not Helen, for the war.
The elders admire Helen's beauty yet wish her gone.
Memorable portrait of Ulysses's plain-looking but overwhelming oratory.

analysis.text: The book contrasts honor and shame, as Hector shames Paris and Helen scorns him, while the gods shape human choices.
The oath scene shows ancient Greek ideas of sacrifice, oaths, and guest-host obligations.

legacy.text: Helen on the wall, the Teichoskopia, became a model for the device of a viewer identifying warriors on a battlefield.

fun_facts.text: Helen's tapestry of the war in sentence 41 is an early example of art depicting a poem's own events.

language_notes.text: "Worsted" means defeated or got the worse of a fight. This is the book's summary heading, which also calls Paris "Alexandria", apparently a slip for Alexandrus.
Cranes were believed to migrate to the edge of the world each winter and war against the Pygmies, a tiny people living by Oceanus.
"Quailed" means shrank back in fear.
"Upbraided" in the previous line means scolded; here "woman-mad" means obsessed with women.
"A shirt of stones" means being stoned to death; Hector says the Trojans are too soft to have punished Paris already.
"Your rebuke is just": Alexandrus (also called Paris) admits Hector's earlier scolding for his cowardice was deserved.
The "gifts of golden Venus" are his beauty and Helen, whom Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) promised him when he judged her the fairest goddess.
Holding his spear by the middle, horizontally, is a signal for a halt, so the Trojans sit and the Achaeans stop shooting.
Sacrificial lambs are offered to seal the oath: a white ram for Sun and a black ewe for Earth, with a third lamb for Jove (the Greek Zeus).
"High-handed" means arrogant and overbearing, so likely to break their word.
Iris takes the form of Laodice, Helen's sister-in-law, because Laodice is married to Helicaon, Antenor's son; the disguise makes the summons seem natural.
"Of the race of Mars" means Hiketaon is descended from the war god; it is a boast of lineage, not literal parentage.
Cicales are cicadas, insects whose shrill, continuous song suits old men who can no longer fight but still talk.
Helen calls Agamemnon her brother-in-law, since he is brother of her husband Menelaus; her self-description as "abhorred" shows her self-loathing.
Priam recalls an earlier campaign in Phrygia, when he fought as ally against the Amazons, a legendary nation of warrior women.
"Ran trippingly on the tongue" means his speech was fluent and quick, free of stumbling.
A churl is a rude, low-born person; here it means a sullen fellow with no polish.
Castor and Pollux are Helen's brothers, later honored as the Dioscuri; Pollux was famed as a boxer, Castor as a horse-tamer.
"The gift of earth" means the wine, a product of the earth's fruitfulness, offered as part of the sacrifice.
"Covenant" means a binding sworn agreement; here it is a truce confirmed by sacrifice and oath.
Wool cut from the lambs' heads was shared out so each prince held a token of the victims while the oath was sworn.
"Thou" and "ye" are archaic forms of address; "rulest" and "seest" are matching old verb endings.
"Reft" is an old past tense of "reave": took away by force.
The wine poured out stands for the brains of oath-breakers: the curse is acted out in the ritual.
"Ilius" is another name for Troy; "wind-beaten" is a standing description of its exposed position.
Lots were shaken in a helmet; the one whose lot leaps out first throws his spear first.
Hector shakes lots in a helmet, looking away to keep the draw fair; the lot that jumps out first gives that man the first throw.
Greaves are shin armor; ancle-clasps are ankle fastenings that held them in place. Cuirass is a breastplate.
Redoubtable means formidable, inspiring fear.
Menelaus refers to Paris's wrong: he stole Helen while a guest in Menelaus's house, breaking the sacred duty of hospitality.
Shirt here means the tunic worn under the armor; the spear tore it but missed the flesh.
Despiteful means spiteful or malicious; Menelaus accuses Jove of cruelty in denying him his revenge.
Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) has just rescued Alexandrus from the duel and set him in his chamber; now she fetches Helen.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, son of Priam; the text uses both names.
Phrygia and Meonia are regions of Asia Minor; Helen sarcastically suggests Venus has another Trojan-side lover waiting for her.
"Hussy" here is a harsh rebuke meaning insolent, shameless woman.
"Laughter-loving" is Venus's standard Homeric epithet.
"Aegis-bearing" describes Jove, who carries the aegis, a fearsome goat-skin shield or cloak; Helen is his daughter in myth.
Cranae is an island where Paris and Helen first spent a night after fleeing Lacedaemon (Sparta).
"Such fine as shall be agreed upon" means compensation to the Achaeans, to be remembered by future generations.

context_notes.text: Alexandrus is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war.
The lyre and handsome looks mark Paris as a lover favored by Venus, in contrast to a warrior.
Menelaus, king of Sparta, is Helen's husband. Alexandrus took her to Troy, which caused the war.
Achaeans and Argives are both names the poem uses for the Greeks.
Talthybius is Agamemnon's herald, who carries messages and handles ceremonial duties.
Aethrae, mother of Theseus, was Helen's attendant; in myth she was taken to Troy after Theseus' abduction of Helen.
The Scaean gates were the main gate of Troy, near which the elders sat and from which the Trojan wall was surveyed.
Before the war, Ulysses and Menelaus came to Troy seeking Helen's peaceful return, but were refused.
Priam is called son of Laomedon, a former king of Troy. Alexandrus is another name for Paris, who took Helen.
Antenor is a respected Trojan elder and counsellor. The Scaean gates were the main gates of Troy facing the plain.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) was king of the gods and guarantor of oaths. Ida is the mountain near Troy where he watched the war.
Dardanus was the legendary ancestor of the Trojan royal line.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and guardian of guests and oaths, so Menelaus rightly appeals to him.
Venus (the Greek Aphrodite), goddess of love, favors Paris, who had judged her the fairest goddess.
Lacedaemon is Sparta, Menelaus's kingdom, where Helen lived before Paris took her to Troy.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) supports the Achaeans; Venus favors Paris.
"Son of Atreus" here is Menelaus; Agamemnon is also a son of Atreus.

literary_notes.text: The noisy Trojans are compared to screaming cranes, setting up a contrast with the silent, disciplined Achaeans.
Menelaus is likened to a hungry lion finding prey, showing his fierce eagerness for vengeance.
Paris's recoil is compared to a man startled by a snake, making his cowardice vivid and almost instinctive.
Hector's taunting question mocks Paris's vanity and shows his contempt for him.
Hector's hardness is compared to a shipwright's axe cutting timber, suggesting his rebuke is steady, tough and cuts exactly as intended.
"Of the loud battle-cry" is Menelaus's stock Homeric epithet, recalling his martial role as he speaks.
Young minds are "light as air", suggesting that the young are fickle, while the old man "looks before and after", weighing past and future.
Helen weaving the war into her tapestry shows her awareness that she is its cause, and makes her an artist of her own story.
The old men are compared to chirping cicadas: their weak but pleasing voices reflect their age and eloquence.
The elders admire her beauty yet wish her gone, showing the tension between her allure and the ruin she brings.
Ulysses is likened to a woolly ram among ewes, conveying his sturdy bulk and command of the ranks.
Ulysses' words fall like winter snow in the wind, a vivid image of his overwhelming, plentiful eloquence after a plain start.
The narrator reveals what Helen cannot know: her brothers are dead, adding pathos to her fear that shame keeps them away.
Comparing the spilled wine to spilled brains makes the oath's penalty vivid and terrible.
The narrator warns that Jove will not fulfil the prayer, hinting that the truce will be broken.
Priam's refusal to watch his son fight shows his fatherly grief and his resigned view of the gods' power.
The fierce-looking warriors and the awed armies create a tense, visual pause before the duel begins.
Menelaus addresses Jove directly in despair, blaming the god for his broken sword and shifting responsibility away from himself.
Venus breaks the strap just as Menelaus is about to win, showing the gods overruling human outcomes.
The parenthetical remark "as a god can do" is a brief aside from the narrator, treating the rescue as easy for a deity.
Venus's flattering description of Paris is a lure, and it contrasts with his actual defeat in the duel.
Helen bitterly tells the goddess to go care for Paris herself, showing her defiance and self-reproach.
Paris's sudden declaration of desire shows his shallowness, and he feels no shame at his defeat.
Comparing the Trojans' hatred of Paris to their hatred of death stresses how despised he is.
